- 7% drop in daily active users

- 2.3 million event records over 18 months
- Need explainable decisions for moderators

**Company brings (C115):**
- 2.3 million records of event data (18 months)
- 5 engineers at up to 20% time
- BehaviorWatch v2 architecture documentation
- AWS EC2/S3 infrastructure

The university side brings semi-supervised anomaly detection expertise, one-class classification methods with known false-positive rates, and concept drift monitoring protocols. This pairing makes sense since the company has data but lacks ML expertise while the researcher needs proprietary high-frequency telemetry, so together they can build something neither could alone.

Now I'm drafting the specific claims: the flagging bottleneck (900 flagged vs 200 reviewable), the 7% DAU drop tied to trust issues, and the false-positive/missed-cheater tradeoff from threshold adjustments as the core problem statements. For what the company brings, I'm listing the 2.3 million event records, five engineers at 20% time, and the AWS EC2/S3 environment.

For the university side, I need to pull from existing findings, and for the "why this pair" reasoning I'm noting the company's ML expertise gap against its data richness, and the researcher's dataset diversity bottleneck that the company's data would resolve.

I'm now working through exact quotes for the problem section, pulling phrases like the 900-account flagging limit and the 7% DAU drop directly from the text. I notice the detail field is in Serbian, though, which complicates quoting since the instructions require 5-20 consecutive words copied exactly — I'll stick to English quotes from the text field where possible.

I'll stick with text for the problem claims—the 900 vs 200 accounts issue and the 7% DAU drop—since those are clearly in English. For the explainability requirement, I may need to cite detail since that's where the Serbian quote about needing clear explanations for flagged accounts lives, and similarly the 2.3 million records figure might only appear there too.

I'm checking whether the term sheet mentions the dataset size directly or if that number only shows up in detail—it looks like the specific "approximately 2.3 million records, 18 months" figure is in the Serbian detail text, so that's what I'll cite for the company's data contribution.

For the problem statement, I'm drafting three facts: the mismatch between 900 daily flagged accounts and the team's capacity to review only 200, the resulting 7% drop in daily active users attributed to trust issues, and the company's lack of expertise to build a better automated model despite having the 18-month, 2.3 million record dataset. I'm reconsidering whether the dataset size really belongs in the problem section versus the company contribution section.

I'll go with three claims, adding the threshold tradeoff as the third problem point since it's grounded in detail text too.

For the structure, I'm organizing problem claims around C115-CH1 (900 vs 200 accounts, 7% DAU drop, threshold tradeoff) and company-brings claims around C115 (dataset size, engineer time allocation, AWS infrastructure).

Now I'm drafting the JSON output, keeping it strictly third-person with no names, no "we," no quotation marks outside quoted figures, and numbers only when sourced. I'm also confirming the dataset figures of 2.3 million records and 18 months are directly quoted and can be used verbatim in the companyBrings sentence.

Now I'm considering the threshold tradeoff claim — whether reducing false positives causing more missed cases counts as an observed fact stated directly in their system's behavior.

For the inference pairings, I'm drafting a claim connecting the company's lack of internal experts for building better decision models to the researcher's bottleneck being access to proprietary telemetry data, pulling from both the company detail about insufficient expertise and the researcher's note on dataset diversity. I'm also noting a factual claim about the researcher's full-cycle work from pipeline design through shadow-mode deployment evaluation of anomaly detection on a live backend, and sketching a third inference tying the company's BehaviorWatch v2 telemetry streams to the detection methods the researcher's work is built to process.

Now I'm brainstorming title options for a manager-facing summary, avoiding numbers or method names — leaning toward something like "Reducing false bans with an explainable anti-cheat system" that captures the business value without technical jargon.

For the research questions, I'm framing future work around which detection method combinations minimize false positives on VoxelRealm's data, what per-account explanations moderators would need, how behavior shifts after patches affect retraining, and how the new pipeline would compare against the current threshold-based logic.

I'm mapping out four plan phases tied to milestones: a data audit and baseline in month one, model prototyping by month three, explainability and workflow integration by month five, and final evaluation and delivery by month six. Now I'm structuring the output as JSON, starting with the title and building out the problem statements with sourced quotes about the review team being overwhelmed and legitimate players getting banned.

I'm adding more facts: the quarterly drop in daily active users attributed to trust issues, and the tradeoff where reducing false positives means missing more real cheating cases. Then I'm moving into the research questions section, starting with which detection methods minimize false positives on the 18-month dataset and what explanation outputs would help moderators act faster.

Now I'm outlining the project plan, starting with a data audit and baseline phase to document the dataset structure and measure the existing system's false-positive rate, followed by a prototype development phase to train and evaluate semi-supervised and one-class models against that baseline.

From there, I'm adding an explainability integration phase to test moderator review workflow usability, and a final phase covering drift monitoring, retraining protocols, and final documentation. I'm also noting what the company is providing—an 18-month dataset of roughly 2.3 million flagged account events.

Now I'm moving into the universityBrings section, noting R0856's expertise in semi-supervised anomaly detection for player behavior telemetry, covering sequence modeling, cheat/bot detection, and behavioral fingerprinting in high-frequency event streams.

One-class classification methods trained only on legitimate sessions achieve good detection performance for scripted clients, while adapting to concept drift in player behavior distributions through dynamic retraining protocols significantly cuts labeling overhead.

Now I'm pairing this with the company's stated lack of internal expertise to build better automated decision models, noting the researcher's bottleneck is access to proprietary telemetry data.

I'm also linking the researcher's full-cycle experience, from data pipeline design to shadow-mode deployment of anomaly detection on a live game backend, with the company's internally built BehaviorWatch v2 system, which generates the kind of high-frequency behavioral telemetry streams that the researcher's detection methods are built to process.

Now I'm double-checking the pairing and phase mapping — confirming the pair id for the "why this pair" entry, and verifying each research question aligns to its correct plan phase: lowest false-positive methods to prototype development, per-account explanations to explainability integration, concept drift to drift monitoring, and the comparison to current systems back to prototype development. I'm also making sure the plan language consistently treats results as delivered without transferring IP ownership.

I'm also running through the remaining compliance checks: no praise or named individuals, no first-person plural pronouns in my own sentences, no stray quotation marks outside quoted material, and verifying that every number appearing in a sentence is backed by a matching number inside its accompanying quote across each problem and benefit statement.

Now I'm checking that the research questions and plan avoid stating facts about the records themselves. I notice RQ1 still references the eighteen-month log span, which crosses into describing the data rather than future work, so I'm revising it to drop that detail and keep the focus purely on which detection methods minimize false positives.

For the threshold tradeoff claim, I'm comparing my translation against the original quote about false positive reduction causing more real cheating to slip through undetected, and confirming the phrasing aligns with the source.

I also want to make sure the subject identifier "C115-CH1" is used consistently throughout. The JSON output should be ready to finalize now.
